title: Hypocrisy and hidden deceit are deadly; every good or evil done to a brother is done to God
english: "Each one speaks peace to his neighbor, but holds enmity within himself," and so on (Jeremiah 9:8). The scribes and Pharisees of the Jewish people would not have inherited so great a "woe" from the Savior if it were not for hypocrisy. For in exposing their sins, the Lord never stopped warning them on every occasion: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites," calling them whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful to people on the outside but inside are full of dead bones and every kind of uncleanness (Matthew 23:27). If we do something good to a neighbor through unhypocritical love, we hear from the Savior: "Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of mine, you did for me" (Matthew 25:40). In the same way, if we do something evil to a brother through deceptive and defiled hypocrisy, or through any other sin whatever, we sin against God just as much. Hypocrisy, brothers, is therefore a terrible and hostile thing. And deceit hidden in the heart, meant to entrap those who come forward in simplicity, speaks one thing with the mouth while carrying another in the breast, and so it deceives those who possess love. Pride is not good, since it carries with it much empty glory. For it is clear—very clear—that every perfect good comes from God. It cannot be received by a human being in any other way, so that what has been said is truly the most certain of all: the one who boasts should glory only in this, in understanding and knowing that the Lord himself is the one who shows mercy and judgment and righteousness, and in this is the will of God (Jeremiah 9:24). For the divine takes pleasure in such a person and always produces good things that are lasting and secure, when that person attributes the cause of the good things he has to the one who is truly the ultimate cause—the one to whom he must also attribute the cause of the good things remaining.

orientation: Gregory opens his commentary on Jeremiah by applying the prophet's warning about a neighbor who speaks peace while harboring enmity to the hypocrisy of the scribes and Pharisees.
